title: Thread Pool Starvation
description: Understand how blocking code and synchronous operations exhaust the .NET thread pool in ASP.NET Core, and learn patterns to prevent thread pool starvation.

data.text: ASP.NET Core runs on a limited number of threads. When too many threads block on I/O—waiting for a database, a file, or `Thread.Sleep`—the thread pool cannot serve new requests. This is **thread pool starvation**, and it causes latency spikes and 503 errors even though the CPU is mostly idle.

The .NET thread pool maintains a minimum number of worker threads and I/O completion port (IOCP) threads. When a thread blocks, the pool eventually adds more threads, but that injection is throttled and takes time. Under sustained load, blocked threads accumulate faster than the pool can replace them, and requests queue.

terms.definition: A thread that executes CPU-bound code in the thread pool.
A thread that processes asynchronous I/O completion callbacks.
A condition where all available threads are blocked or busy, causing new work to wait indefinitely.

data.title: Blocking Code That Causes Starvation
data.content: Using `Task.Wait()` or `.Result` inside an ASP.NET Core request blocks a thread for the entire duration of an async operation.

data.text: If your application must call legacy synchronous libraries, you can raise the thread pool minimum with `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads`. This is a mitigation, not a cure—more threads mean more context switching and memory pressure. The better approach is to remove the blocking calls or run them on a background queue.

data.title: Setting Minimum Threads
data.content: Increase the worker and IOCP thread minimums during application startup.

rows: Blocks thread for full I/O duration

data.title: Deadlocks from sync-over-async
data.text: Calling `.Wait()` on an async method that captures the synchronization context can deadlock the entire app. In ASP.NET Core, use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in libraries, and never block on async code in request handlers.

data.title: Key Takeaway
points: Thread pool starvation happens when blocking calls hold threads longer than the pool can replace them.
Prefer async/await all the way down; avoid `.Result`, `.Wait()`, and `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` in request paths.
Use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in class libraries to prevent synchronization context capture.
Background queues and `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads` are mitigations, not replacements for correct async code.
data.takeaway: A blocked thread is a wasted thread. In ASP.NET Core, blocking one thread costs you the entire request latency.
